newsitem.title: USA: Cuba, US conclude talks on migration accords.
newsitem.headline: Cuba, US conclude talks on migration accords.

text.p: The United States and Cuba on Thursday concluded two days of talks on migration, reiterating their commitment to full implementation of accords signed in recent years, the State Department said.

Spokesman Nicholas Burns said the United States had met its goal of issuing 20,000 travel authorisations in each of the first two years since a September 1994 joint communique, and expected to meet that goal again this year.

"These accords are deterring the dangerous outflow of migrants in unseaworthy vessels. At the same time they are greatly expanding opportunities for safe, legal and orderly migration from Cuba to the United States," Burns said in a statement.

The latest talks on migration, one of the few areas in which Washington and Havana cooperate, started days after Cuba charged that people in the United States were behind the bombing of two hotels in Havana last weekend and withdrew its baseball team from a series against the United States in Connecticut.
The U.S. government said the charges were unsupported.

The U.S. and Cuban delegations met at the U.S. mission to the United Nations in New York, focusing in their discussions on technical matters related to the agreements of September 1994 and May 1995. The last such discussions took place in Havana last December.
Burns said the delegations had a "comprehensive, constructive, and frank discussion" and the atmosphere in the talks was businesslike. The talks would be continued on a regular basis, he said.

Under the 1995 agreement, Washington undertook to repatriate Cuban boat people intercepted trying to reach the United States, while at the same time increasing the number of visas it grants Cubans to 20,000 a year.

The aim, largely achieved, was to halt a flow of Cuban boat people over the Florida Straits that reached crisis point in August 1994 when more than 30,000 Cubans left the communist-ruled island on flimsy rafts.
The two countries, which have no diplomatic relations, have been political enemies since the 1959 revolution that brought Cuban President Fidel Castro to power.

The U.S. delegation to the New York talks was led by John Hamilton, assistant secretary of state for Central American, Caribbean and Cuban affairs. Cuban parliamentary president Ricardo Alarcon heads the Cuban side.
